Parent priority #3: smallest fp32 workload, grid=1 program, isolates the per-call fixed cost with no device work.

performance_interpretation: NO PROFILER COUNTERS WERE OBTAINED. Six collection attempts (5 workloads, levels metrics and source) all returned the identical error 'msprof base collection exited successfully without profile completion marker', with summary.stage_count=1, metrics={}, artifacts=[] and empty capabilities on every result. The service still declares NPU/msprof profiling supported with performance_counters, pipeline_utilization, kernel_profile and instruction_listing, and the target was healthy (1 device slot available, 0 broken probes), so this is a collection/packaging failure in the msprof wrapper, not a capability gap. Consequently none of the requested hardware facts (kernel duration vs full call, MTE2/MTE3/vector busy times, physical bytes) could be measured. The following is derived from the authoritative eval evidence in get_profile_context plus the frozen workload specs in hgkda_workloads, and is inference, not measurement. (1) Two clearly separated regimes exist. The nine 1024..1048576-element workloads are flat in latency: fp32 29.097 / 29.022 / 29.286 us at n=1024 / 65536 / 1048576 (spread 0.264 us, 0.9%), and fp16 25.121 / 25.209 / 26.388 us. At the effective rate the 4096x4096 cases themselves demonstrate (1.295 TB/s), the fp32 1M case moves 8.39 MB of logical traffic, i.e. about 6.5 us of device work, yet timing-10 is not slower than timing-8 by any resolvable margin. That ~6.5 us of device work being invisible means the per-call fixed cost (launch + allocation + Python prelude) is paid on the CPU side and is larger than the device work for all nine - a launch/parallelism regime. The three 4096x4096 workloads scale with bytes instead: doubling logical bytes from 67.1 MB (fp16/bf16) to 134.2 MB (fp32) raises latency from 42.83/44.45 us to 103.65 us, a device-bound regime. Because the two regimes have different limits this is a mixed operator at a per-workload scope, but dominant_bound is recorded as unknown since no counter attributes it. (2) Effective logical rates (logical bytes / eval latency, NOT measured physical HBM bytes, and confounded by L2: the device reports 176160768 B of L2 and all three working sets plus 100 repeated iterations on the same buffers fit inside it): timing-3 fp16 67.108864 MB / 0.04282751 ms = 1.567 TB/s (391.7 Gelem/s, or 19.59 Gelem/s per AI core over the 20 cores); timing-7 bf16 67.108864 MB / 0.04444857 ms = 1.510 TB/s; timing-11 fp32 134.217728 MB / 0.10365273 ms = 1.295 TB/s (161.9 Gelem/s). References for contrast: timing-11 1.115 TB/s, timing-3 and timing-7 both 0.272 TB/s. (3) Answering parent priority #2: timing-3 at 1.567 TB/s is the fastest effective rate observed anywhere in this snapshot, and its bf16 sibling at 1.510 TB/s agrees within 4%. Under the hypothesis that this band is the achievable effective movement rate on this device for L2-resident 2-byte data, timing-3 is already at that limit and has little headroom; claiming more would require exceeding the fastest rate the same candidate achieves on identical-bytes input, which this evidence does not support. Note the fp16 tile is not the cheapest in UB terms (32 KiB source + 64 KiB fp32 intermediate + 32 KiB result = 128 KiB) versus fp32 (32+32+32 = 96 KiB), yet it is faster, which argues against a UB-capacity limit in this regime. (4) Answering parent priority #1: timing-11 is the only workload with a quantified device-side gap. Its 1.295 TB/s is 17.4% below timing-3's 1.567 TB/s on the same element count; at 1.567 TB/s, 134.2 MB would take 85.7 us instead of 103.65 us, i.e. up to 17.5 us and a speedup near 1.40 instead of 1.1617. Two candidate causes are indistinguishable without counters: (a) per-program overhead, because fp32 runs 2048 programs of BLOCK=8192 while fp16 runs 1024 of BLOCK=16384 over the same 16.78M elements; (b) vector-issue throughput, since a 4-byte vector op retires half the elements per instruction, which would also produce a ~2x step (fp32 is 2.42x fp16) and would make a bigger tile useless. The 2.42x step is slightly larger than the 2.0x byte ratio, which is the margin each hypothesis has to explain. A BLOCK=16384 experiment (the naive reading of the parent's suggestion) is additionally UB-risky: 16384 fp32 elements staged as source + fp32 temp + result is 64+64+64 = 192 KiB, exactly the available UB, and the bounded historical prior records an fp32 BLOCK=32768 flip candidate requiring 384 KiB against 192 KiB available and overflowing. (5) Answering parent priority #3: the profiler could not separate device kernel duration from full call; the only quantitative handle is the flatness argument in (1), which bounds the device share at roughly <=6.5 us for timing-10 and ~0 for timing-8 (grid=1, 4 KiB), so at most ~22% of the 29.3 us call. The remaining fixed cost tracks the torch reference, which also pays 26.72-26.87 us on the same three inputs, so the harness per-iteration overhead is shared and our realizable margin on the small group is only the 2.34-2.42 us that separate us from the C++ reference. (6) geo_mean arithmetic, because it changes the ranking the parent proposed. Geo_mean weights every workload with the same 1/12 exponent, so what matters is relative latency reduction per workload, not absolute size. The nine-workload speedup set (1.0140, 0.9789, 0.9621, 0.9369, 0.9322, 0.8932, 0.9184, 0.9193, 0.9174) has a geometric mean of 0.9408, so bringing all nine to exact reference parity is worth only (1/0.9408)^(9/12) = 1.0475, i.e. geo_mean 1.2911 -> ~1.352, and that ceiling is not reachable because the three fp16 cases are already at parity (1.014/0.979/0.962) and only the six fp32/bf16 cases carry the ~8% gap. Against that, the timing-11 gap in (4) is worth (1.40/1.1617)^(1/12) = 1.0156 by itself. So the parent's premise that the nine small cases dominate is true of their count but bounded by the fact that their achievable reduction is <=8% each, of which an unquantifiable part correlates with run order rather than with our code: our host prelude is dtype-independent, yet the candidate runs 25.6 us (fp16), 26.3 us (bf16) and 29.1 us (fp32) on the 1024-element case where the plan is grid=1, BLOCK=1024 and 4 KiB of data in all three - a 3.5 us spread our code cannot produce, while the reference spreads 25.2/24.2/26.8 us over the same cases. Chasing the fp32/bf16 small-case residual therefore risks optimizing measurement state.

next_experiment.action_description: In the 4-byte path only (y.element_size() >= 4), make each program process two consecutive BLOCK tiles in a loop instead of one, halving the program count without changing the UB footprint: grid = ceil(n / (BLOCK * ITERS)) with ITERS=2, and inside the kernel for i in tl.static_range(ITERS): offs = (tl.program_id(0) * ITERS + i) * BLOCK + tl.arange(0, BLOCK) with the existing per-tile mask kept. For timing-11 (n=16777216, BLOCK=8192) this moves 2048 programs to 1024 - exactly what the fp16 sibling already runs - while per-program staged bytes stay at 96 KiB (32 KiB source + 32 KiB fp32 temp + 32 KiB result), so it stays clear of the 192 KiB UB wall that the BLOCK=16384 variant would hit at exactly 192 KiB. Do NOT change the 2-byte path in this experiment; timing-3 and timing-7 are already at the top of the observed effective-rate band. Leave _pick_block, the masked/unmasked split, the strided kernel and the launch closure untouched.
next_experiment.expected_impact: If the fp32 4096x4096 deficit is per-program overhead, timing-11 should move from 103.65 us toward the 85.7 us implied by the 1.567 TB/s sibling rate, lifting its speedup from 1.1617 to roughly 1.28-1.40 and geo_mean from 1.2911 to about 1.30-1.31 (+0.9 to +1.6%). If the deficit is instead vector-issue throughput for 4-byte elements, latency will not improve measurably and the hypothesis is cleanly falsified at near-zero cost, which is the more valuable outcome; that result would redirect effort to the six fp32/bf16 small workloads or to accepting timing-11 as-is.
next_experiment.risks_and_rollback: Main risk is masked-path correctness: with ITERS=2 the second tile of the last program can lie entirely past n, so the per-tile mask must be applied per iteration and the load must keep other=1.0 to preserve the HAS_LOG xlogy semantics. Smallest live n that uses the 4-byte path is 1025 and 63 (7x9) in the correctness set, and odd tails such as 1025 must still compute every element exactly once; the covered-range invariant to check is grid * ITERS * BLOCK >= n and that the union of the per-iteration masks is exactly [0, n). Do not touch the strided path or the alignment fallback. Rollback is one constant, ITERS=1, restoring contiguous single-tile mapping byte-for-byte, or revert to the round-0002 candidate at /data/hanle/ascend-optimization/runs/next25-20261029-v2/kg-runs/xlogy_scalar_tensor-next25-20261029-v2-attempt-1/stages/optimize/work/.kernelgen/evals/round-0002/main.py (solution_sha256 5858b8c97b8e7b05382be672f5af129566b1be90f058cf564cb0e002f27b78d9).

All numeric byte rates in this analysis are logical traffic (element count x element size x 2) divided by eval latency. They are NOT measured physical HBM bytes and must not be called achieved bandwidth; the device reports 176160768 B of L2 and every working set here fits inside it across 100 repeated iterations on the same buffers.

The 2.34-2.42 us fp32/bf16 small-workload deficit versus the C++ torch reference is partly confounded with run order: the candidate's dtype-independent host prelude yields 25.6/26.3/29.1 us for fp16/bf16/fp32 on the identical grid=1, BLOCK=1024, 4 KiB case, while the reference moves only 25.2/24.2/26.8 us over the same cases.

The naive BLOCK=16384 fp32 variant requested by the parent would stage 64 KiB source + 64 KiB fp32 intermediate + 64 KiB result = 192 KiB, exactly the available UB; the bounded historical prior records an fp32 BLOCK=32768 candidate needing 384 KiB against 192 KiB available that overflowed, so that variant needs a distinct overflow check before being trusted.

open_questions: Is the 17.4% fp32 4096x4096 deficit caused by 2048-program scheduling overhead or by 4-byte vector-issue throughput (half the elements per instruction)? The ITERS=2 experiment separates these, but only a successful msprof collection would name the limiter directly.

Why does the msprof base collection abort before writing a completion marker on this target? A repeat attempt after the scheduler shows a fully idle device, or a check of whether the candidate's direct raw-launcher path (which bypasses JITFunction.run) is what the msprof wrapper waits on, would decide whether future rounds can rely on profiler evidence at all.

Is the ~3.5 us fp32-versus-fp16 spread on identical-shape 1024-element workloads genuine device cost or benchmark run-order drift? A same-run interleaved measurement of the two dtypes would settle it and would tell the Coder whether the six fp32/bf16 small workloads have any real headroom.
